usage: Go-to line at the clinic or pharmacy
Written as one word — 손목 (wrist) + 시계 (watch)
시큰거리다 describes a dull joint ache
examples: 마우스를 오래 써서 손목이 너무 아파요.
My wrist really hurts from using the mouse too long.
The classic desk-job complaint
넘어지면서 손목을 짚어서 삐었어요.
I sprained my wrist catching myself when I fell.
짚다 = to brace/prop with your hand
손목에 무리가 가지 않게 보호대를 차세요.
Wear a brace so you don't strain your wrist.
무리가 가다 = to put strain on
nuance: 손목 is the joint where the hand (손) meets the arm. Korean stacks 손 + 목, so think 'hand-neck.' Office workers use it constantly to describe RSI-type pain from keyboards and phones, so it is genuinely useful at the doctor.
mistakes: Don't confuse 손목 (wrist) with 목 (neck) — 목 alone means your neck/throat.
It's a body part, not the watch itself; the watch is 손목시계.

usage: The single most common ankle complaint
examples: 계단에서 발목을 삐어서 절뚝거리며 걸었어요.
I sprained my ankle on the stairs and walked with a limp.
절뚝거리다 = to limp
발목이 부어서 신발이 안 들어가요.
My ankle is so swollen my shoe won't fit.
Very real after a sprain
등산 갈 때는 발목을 잡아주는 신발을 신으세요.
Wear shoes that support your ankle when you go hiking.
잡아주다 = to support/hold
nuance: 발목 is 발 (foot) + 목 (neck), the joint above your foot. Ankle sprains are extremely common, so 발목을 삐다 is a phrase you'll hear and use at orthopedic clinics (정형외과) all the time. It also shows up when talking about pant length.
mistakes: Don't say 발 아파요 when you specifically twisted the ankle — use 발목 to be precise.
Remember 붓다 is ㅅ-irregular: 부어요 / 부었어요, not 붓어요.

examples: 테니스를 친 뒤로 팔꿈치가 계속 아파요.
My elbow has been hurting ever since I played tennis.
'Tennis elbow' is a real diagnosis here too
책상에 팔꿈치를 괴고 졸았어요.
I dozed off propped up on my elbow on the desk.
Common posture in a boring meeting
좁은 지하철에서 옆 사람 팔꿈치에 부딪혔어요.
I bumped into the next person's elbow on the crowded subway.
부딪히다 = to collide/bump
nuance: 팔꿈치 is the elbow joint. The spelling trips people up — it's 팔(arm) + 꿈치, written as one word with the double consonant ㄲ. You'll need it for joint pain, for describing crowded subway jostling, and for posture.
mistakes: A frequent misspelling is 팔꿉치 or 팔굼치 — the correct form is 팔꿈치.
Don't drop the 팔 and just say 꿈치; the full word is 팔꿈치.

examples: 밤에 문턱에 새끼발가락을 찧어서 너무 아팠어요.
I stubbed my pinky toe on the door frame at night and it hurt so much.
A universally painful experience
발가락 사이가 가려운 걸 보니 무좀인 것 같아요.
It's itchy between my toes, so I think it's athlete's foot.
무좀 = athlete's foot
신발이 작아서 발가락이 꽉 끼어요.
The shoes are small so my toes feel cramped.
꽉 끼다 = to be tight/cramped
nuance: 발가락 means toe (발 foot + 가락 digit), parallel to 손가락 (finger). Use 엄지발가락 for the big toe and 새끼발가락 for the pinky toe. It's practical for shoe-fitting and for the very common foot issues like 무좀.
mistakes: Don't mix up 발가락 (toe) with 발톱 (toenail) — the nail is 발톱.
It's 발가락, not 발까락; the spelling uses ㄱ not ㄲ.

examples: 스쿼트를 했더니 허벅지가 너무 아파요.
My thighs are so sore after doing squats.
근육통 (muscle soreness) talk
청바지가 허벅지에서 꽉 껴요.
The jeans are tight around the thighs.
A real fitting problem
오래 앉아 있으면 허벅지가 저려요.
My thighs go numb if I sit too long.
저리다 = to go numb/tingle
nuance: 허벅지 is the thick upper part of the leg, the thigh. It comes up constantly at the gym (스쿼트, 런지) and when clothes don't fit right. For the inner thigh say 허벅지 안쪽, and for the back of the thigh 허벅지 뒤.
mistakes: Don't confuse 허벅지 (thigh) with 종아리 (calf) — the calf is the lower leg.
허벅지 is informal-neutral; in a medical setting you might also hear 대퇴부, but 허벅지 is what people actually say.

usage: 쥐가 나다 = to get a cramp
Common after a long day standing
examples: 하이힐을 신었더니 종아리가 너무 뭉쳤어요.
My calves got really tight from wearing high heels.
Familiar end-of-day complaint
자다가 종아리에 쥐가 나서 깼어요.
I woke up because I got a cramp in my calf.
쥐가 나다 = sudden cramp
많이 걸어서 종아리가 퉁퉁 부었어요.
My calves are all swollen from walking a lot.
퉁퉁 붓다 = to swell up
nuance: 종아리 is the back muscle of the lower leg, the calf. You'll hear it for cramps (쥐가 나다), for tightness after standing or walking, and at massage shops. 종아리 알 refers specifically to the bulge of the calf muscle.
mistakes: Don't swap 종아리 (calf) and 정강이 (shin); the shin is the hard front bone.
쥐가 나다 (to cramp) is idiomatic — don't translate 쥐 (mouse) literally.

examples: 침대 모서리에 정강이를 부딪혀서 멍이 들었어요.
I banged my shin on the corner of the bed and got a bruise.
멍이 들다 = to bruise
축구하다가 상대 선수한테 정강이를 차였어요.
I got kicked in the shin by the opposing player during soccer.
차이다 = to get kicked
정강이는 살이 없어서 부딪히면 정말 아파요.
The shin has no padding, so it really hurts when you hit it.
살이 없다 = to have no flesh/padding
nuance: 정강이 is the hard bony front of the lower leg, the shin — the opposite side from 종아리 (calf). Because it's all bone with little cushioning, hitting it on furniture is a sharp, memorable pain everyone relates to. The bone itself is 정강이뼈.
mistakes: Don't confuse 정강이 (front shin) with 종아리 (back calf).
When you got hit, use the passive 차이다/부딪히다 (got kicked/bumped), not the active form.

usage: I got hit on the back of the head
to feel eyes on the back of one's head
examples: 선반 모서리에 뒤통수를 부딪혀서 혹이 났어요.
I hit the back of my head on the shelf corner and got a bump.
혹이 나다 = to get a lump
믿었던 친구한테 뒤통수를 맞았어요.
I got stabbed in the back by a friend I trusted.
Figurative — betrayal
한국 사람들은 뒤통수가 예쁜 걸 신경 써요.
Koreans care about having a nicely shaped back of the head.
A real cultural beauty point
nuance: 뒤통수 literally means the back of the head (뒤 back + 통수). Beyond the physical sense, 뒤통수를 치다/맞다 is an extremely common idiom for betraying or being betrayed — worth knowing both meanings. Koreans also genuinely comment on whether someone's 뒤통수 is round or flat (납작하다).
mistakes: Don't take 뒤통수를 맞았어요 literally if the context is social — it usually means 'I got betrayed.'
It's casual; in formal/medical speech you'd say 뒷머리 or 후두부 instead.

examples: 면접 때 너무 긴장해서 손바닥에 땀이 났어요.
My palms got sweaty because I was so nervous at the interview.
Relatable nerves
우리 집은 손바닥만 해서 짐 둘 데가 없어요.
Our place is tiny (palm-sized), so there's nowhere to put stuff.
손바닥만 하다 = very small
넘어질 때 손바닥으로 바닥을 짚었어요.
I braced my fall with my palms.
짚다 = to brace/prop
nuance: 손바닥 is the palm, the inner surface of the hand (손 hand + 바닥 floor/flat surface). The opposite, the back of the hand, is 손등. 손바닥만 하다 ('palm-sized') is a handy idiom for describing something very small, like a cramped apartment.
mistakes: Don't confuse 손바닥 (palm) with 손등 (back of the hand).
손바닥만 하다 is figurative for 'tiny' — not a literal measurement.

usage: I got a blister on my sole
examples: 하루 종일 걸었더니 발바닥이 불이 나는 것 같아요.
After walking all day, my soles feel like they're on fire.
불이 나다 = to burn (figurative)
새 구두를 신고 발바닥에 물집이 잡혔어요.
I got blisters on my soles from new dress shoes.
Break-in pain
발바닥 마사지를 받으니까 피로가 풀려요.
A foot-sole massage relieves my fatigue.
피로가 풀리다 = fatigue eases
nuance: 발바닥 is the sole, the bottom flat surface of the foot (발 foot + 바닥 flat surface), mirroring 손바닥. It comes up after long days of walking, with blisters (물집), and at foot-massage or 지압 shops, which are popular in Korea.
mistakes: Don't confuse 발바닥 (sole) with 발등 (top of the foot).
물집이 잡히다 / 물집이 생기다 (to form a blister) is the natural collocation — not 물집을 만들다.

examples: 여름엔 겨드랑이에 땀이 너무 많이 나요.
My armpits sweat way too much in summer.
Korea's humid summers
땀 냄새 때문에 겨드랑이에 데오드란트를 발라요.
I put deodorant on my armpits because of sweat odor.
데오드란트 = deodorant
겨드랑이에 멍울이 만져져서 병원에 갔어요.
I felt a lump in my armpit so I went to the hospital.
멍울 = lump (lymph node)
nuance: 겨드랑이 is the armpit/underarm. It's very practical in Korea's hot, humid summers when talking about sweat (땀) and odor (냄새), and it also comes up with deodorant, hair removal (제모), and noticing lumps. The spelling with -랑이 is worth memorizing.
mistakes: A common misspelling is 겨드랑 or 겨드량이 — the standard form is 겨드랑이.
For 'I sweat,' use 땀이 나다 (sweat comes out), not 땀을 하다.

usage: to sit down and stay put
to be slow to get up / a homebody
examples: 딱딱한 의자에 오래 앉아서 엉덩이가 아파요.
My bottom hurts from sitting on a hard chair too long.
Office-life complaint
공부 잘하려면 엉덩이를 오래 붙이고 있어야 해요.
To study well you have to keep your butt in the chair a long time.
엉덩이를 붙이다 = to sit and persevere
요즘 엉덩이 운동으로 스쿼트를 하고 있어요.
I've been doing squats as a glute workout lately.
Fitness context
nuance: 엉덩이 is the buttocks/bottom and the general hip-seat area. It's an everyday, non-vulgar word used for sitting-related soreness, for fitness (엉덩이 운동), and in idioms like 엉덩이가 무겁다 (a homebody / slow to move) and 엉덩이를 붙이다 (to settle in and stick with a task).
mistakes: 엉덩이 is neutral and fine in normal conversation; 궁둥이 is more casual/childish for the same area — stick with 엉덩이.
Don't confuse it with 허리 (waist/lower back); back pain is 허리, seat soreness is 엉덩이.
